newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU leaders face decisions on bloc's future.
newsitem.headline: EU leaders face decisions on bloc's future.

text.p: Europe's future, from its single currency to a treaty to allow it to expand eastwards, tops the agenda of European Union leaders at their year-end summit in Dublin this week.

Aiming to give, in European Commission President Jacques Santer's words, a "strong and clear signal that Europe is on the move," the leaders are set to study three reports on the new currency and a draft treaty to prepare for the 21st century.

Both moves are essential if the 15-nation bloc is to reach its goals of having a shared currency, the Euro, by January 1, 1999, and to open its doors early in the next century to a wave of new members from central and eastern Europe.
In the short term, the bloc has not yet even agreed on the single-currency papers the leaders are supposed to look at at the two-day summit, which begins on Friday.
Fears in Germany that once countries have joined a single currency they will give up on fiscal discipline have caused Bonn to insist on a stringent stability pact for post-Euro economies.

It wants steep fines levied on countries that let their budget deficits grow unless there are special circumstances forcing such growth. It also wants specific, quantifiable language to define those circumstances.

EU finance ministers have agreed on the fines, but are still at odds over the circumstances. Failure to agree last week forced the ministers to call a special meeting in Dublin on Thursday, on the eve of the summit to sort it out.

Assuming they do -- and both Germany and EU president Ireland say this is likely -- the leaders will be able to underline to financial markets their commitment to keep sound economies after economic and monetary union.

The other Euro reports, already informally agreed, lay out the legal basis for the new currency and proposals for a voluntary exchange rate mechanism to keep currencies outside the Euro zone stable with those inside.
The Irish EU presidency is holding its breath that initial, generally positive reaction to its draft treaty will hold through the summit.

Unveiled last week, the draft is designed as a working document for negotiators over the next six months as they try to to meet a June deadline for completing a new treaty. Six months later, enlargement negotiations are to begin.
The EU is aiming for closer cooperation in crime fighting, a commitment to higher employment, stronger foreign policy links and a true border-free Europe with common asylum and immigration policies.
Ireland deliberately wrote the treaty in a way that allows countries that disagree with what is in it, notably Britain, to accept it as a snapshot of where negotiations stand.
At a meeting of foreign ministers in Brussels on Friday, most countries gave cautious approval to the draft.
French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette said the report reflected an unambitious agenda and hinted that France would demand more at the summit.
Whether this will happen will become clearer after French President Jacques Chirac and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl meet in Nuremburg on Monday.

Britain also remains a wild card. Although Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said the draft was fair, Prime Minister John Major is under intense pressure from Euro-sceptics in his ruling Conservative party.
They will be watching every move he makes in Dublin.
